questions.question: What is the Open Study Buddy?
questions.answer: The Open Study Buddy device is a desk companion that you build yourself from a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, a 360 × 360 round color display, an INMP441 digital microphone, a MAX98357A amplifier with a small speaker, and three push buttons named **Mode**, **Up**, and **Down**. It listens to a spoken question, shows what it heard on the round screen, speaks an answer aloud, and tells you what is due and when your next test is. The device is an **agent terminal**: it gives an agent a face, a voice, ears, and buttons, while the agent's "thinking" happens on a **buddy server** that your class or school runs. Every line of MicroPython on the Pico is code you write. By the end of the course the device can show a clock and your school mascot, draw a live spectrum of sound, record push-to-talk questions, receive "test tomorrow" alerts over MQTT, and announce events from the school calendar. See [Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md) and the [Course Description](course-description.md).

questions.question: Who is this course for?
questions.answer: The primary audience is high school students in grades 9–12. The material is also accessible to motivated junior high students, college undergraduates, coding clubs, hobbyists, and the teachers and mentors who run school maker programs. The book assumes you have already taken *Learning MicroPython and Physical Computing* or have equivalent experience. That means you can flash MicroPython onto a Pico, use Thonny and the REPL, write loops, functions, and modules, read a debounced push button, and drive a display. No prior experience with signal processing, networking, or artificial intelligence is assumed; those are taught from the ground up. Basic arithmetic and the idea of a sine wave are helpful. Teachers will find a separate [Teacher's Guide](learning-graph/teachers-guide/index.md) with a purchasing guide for classroom kits.

questions.question: What do I need to know before I start?
questions.answer: You should already be comfortable with the basic Pico workflow: flashing MicroPython, running code from **Thonny** or `mpremote`, typing at the **REPL**, and writing small programs with loops, functions, and imports. You should have read a button and driven a display at least once. If any of that feels rusty, [Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems](chapters/02-micropython-review/index.md) is a fast refresher. It covers the REPL, modules and imports, the config file pattern, `boot.py` and `main.py`, the `mip` package manager, the `machine` library, GPIO pins, timers, interrupts, memory limits, garbage collection, and byte arrays. It is a tune-up, not a first introduction, so if every topic there is new, take the prerequisite course first. You do not need to know anything about audio, the FFT, Wi-Fi, HTTP, or MQTT. Each of those is introduced in its own chapter, in the order the device needs it.

questions.question: What parts are in the kit and what does each one do?
questions.answer: The base kit has five functional parts plus wiring supplies: | Part | Job | |------|-----| | Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | The brain: runs your MicroPython and connects to Wi-Fi | | 2.1 inch round display (GC9B72 controller) | The face: 360 × 360 pixels of text, clock, mascot, and meters | | INMP441 microphone board | The ears: turns room sound into digital numbers over I2S | | MAX98357A amplifier and speaker | The voice: turns digital audio into sound | | Three push buttons | The hands: Mode, Up, and Down | A breadboard, Dupont wires, and a USB cable connect and power everything, so no soldering is required. Together the parts cost a few tens of dollars. A common misconception is that the Pico contains the microphone or speaker; it does not. The conversion from sound to numbers happens on the microphone board, and the amplifier drives the speaker. See [Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md) and the [Kit Parts Infographic](sims/kit-parts-infographic/index.md). Prices and search terms are in the [Teacher's Guide](learning-graph/teachers-guide/index.md).

questions.question: How much does it cost to build one?
questions.answer: The parts in the base kit cost a few tens of dollars in total, which is the point of the project: a personal agent device that a school can afford to put on many desks. The most expensive single parts are usually the Pico 2 W and the round display. The microphone, amplifier, speaker, buttons, breadboard, and wires are each inexpensive commodity parts. There is no subscription fee. Commercial personal agents usually bill monthly and run on a vendor's computers. The Open Study Buddy's agent runs on hardware the class or school controls, such as a Raspberry Pi in the library or a teacher's laptop, and the starter buddy server uses only Python's standard library. If you plan to buy for a classroom, the [Teacher's Guide](learning-graph/teachers-guide/index.md) includes a purchasing guide with single-unit, classroom-of-20, and district-scale estimates, plus the search keywords that find each part.

questions.question: How is this book organized?
questions.answer: The book has 18 chapters, and each one adds one idea on top of the previous chapter and ends with a working device feature. The order follows the dependencies between the book's 326 concepts: 1. **Foundations (Chapters 1–4):** personal agents, a MicroPython review, sound and digital audio, and the hardware kit. 2. **Display and controls (Chapters 5–7):** pixels and color, drawing directly to display regions, buttons, and the device-mode state machine. 3. **Audio and DSP (Chapters 8–12):** I2S audio, the FFT, high-performance MicroPython, microphone calibration with push-to-talk, and wake-word detection. 4. **Network and agent (Chapters 13–16):** Wi-Fi and HTTP, streaming and security, MQTT push alerts, and the school agent and calendar. 5. **Responsibility and integration (Chapters 17–18):** privacy and responsible listening, then testing, integration, and capstone projects. The [List of Chapters](chapters/index.md) has a summary of each. The [Learning Graph Viewer](sims/graph-viewer/index.md) shows how the concepts depend on each other.

questions.question: How should I use this textbook?
questions.answer: Work through the chapters in order, because each depends on the ones before it. Within a chapter, read a section, then run the test script it names on your own kit before moving on. The book is honest about what has and has not been measured, so your own measurements are part of the lesson. Use the MicroSims. Almost every chapter embeds interactive simulations, such as the [FFT Bin Calculator](sims/fft-bin-calculator/index.md) or the [Device Mode State Machine](sims/device-mode-state-machine/index.md), that let you practice the arithmetic or the logic before you touch hardware. The full set is on the [List of MicroSims](sims/index.md). When you meet an unfamiliar term, check the [Glossary](glossary.md). When a build step fails, look in the "Common Challenge Questions" section of this FAQ and in [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md), which teaches probes, self-tests, and the three classic failures.

questions.question: Who is Sage the Owl?
questions.answer: Sage is the book's learning mascot: a slate-blue owl with a cream chest and small round orange-framed glasses. Sage's catchphrase is "Let's listen closely!" and Sage calls students "builders." Sage has no gender, so the book uses "Sage" or *they/them*. Sage appears only when they have a specific job to do, and each pose signals a different job: 1. **Welcome** opens a chapter and explains why it matters. 2. **Thinking** marks a key idea or mental model. 3. **Tip** offers a shortcut or best practice. 4. **Warning** heads off a common mistake and gives the fix. 5. **Encouraging** appears at a notoriously hard topic. 6. **Celebration** names what you just mastered at the end of a chapter. When you see Sage, slow down: the admonition is a signal, not decoration. Sage introduces themselves fully at the start of [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md).

questions.question: How long does the course take?
questions.answer: The book is designed so that each of the 18 chapters ends with a working feature, which makes a chapter a natural unit for a week of class or a club meeting series. A full school year is a comfortable pace for a class that builds every test and attempts a capstone. A motivated individual with the prerequisite skills can move faster, especially through the refresher material in Chapters 1 and 2. The time varies most with hands-on work. Wiring and verifying the kit in [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md) is usually quick if you follow the wire-one-part-then-test order. Chapters that ask you to measure your own board, such as microphone calibration in [Chapter 11](chapters/11-mic-calibration-push-to-talk/index.md) and threshold tuning in [Chapter 12](chapters/12-wake-word-detection/index.md), take longer because the measurement is the learning. Plan extra time for the capstone in [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md).

questions.question: Do I need to know about artificial intelligence or LLMs?
questions.answer: No. The book teaches the agent side in steps called **agent progression levels**, and the first level uses no AI model at all: | Level | Brain | What it adds | |-------|-------|--------------| | 1 | A rule-based buddy server, about 100 lines, no LLM | Fixed rules that read the school calendar | | 2 | The same server plus speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and one LLM call | Spoken input and output, free-form questions | | 3 | An optional open-source agent framework behind the same contract | Planning loop, memory, and approval rules | You can finish a fully working device at Level 1, with a **rule-based agent** whose replies come from fixed rules. Because the device and server share one small **request-reply contract**, the Pico code is identical at all three levels. The book does not cover building or training language models or speech recognizers; it relies on a separate service for transcription. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md), the [Agent Progression Level Explorer](sims/agent-progression-level-explorer/index.md), and [Chapter 16](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md).

questions.question: Can my school have its own customized Study Buddy?
questions.answer: Yes. Per-school customization is a core design goal. A school changes one configuration file, `agent.toml`, and nothing in the code. That file holds the school's name and id, its time zone, the calendar source, its courses, which features are on, reminder timing, greeting voice and prompts, the mascot image, and the wake phrase. A school can give its device its own **school mascot**, such as Gale the Griffin at the example Cedar Ridge High School, drawn on the round display. It can choose a custom wake phrase like "Hey Griffin" and its own color theme. The school's calendar drives announcements for tests and project due dates. See [Chapter 16: Configuring the School Agent and Calendar](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md) and the [Schools](schools/index.md) section, which shows several example school editions.

questions.question: Where can I find the code for each chapter?
questions.answer: Each chapter names its test scripts, such as `05-display-basics/01-fill-timing.py` or `13-wifi-http-agent-link/server/buddy_server.py`. The scripts live in the book's GitHub repository under `src/chapters/`, one folder per chapter. The base kit's shared code, including `config.py` with the pin assignments, lives under `src/kits/study-buddy-base/`. Each chapter folder has a `README.md` that says what a passing run looks like for every script, and `src/chapters/README.md` explains how to upload and run them with Thonny or `mpremote`. Server-side programs, such as the buddy server and its tests, run on your computer or a school Raspberry Pi, not on the Pico. The repository is linked from the top of every page of this site. Start with the kit's numbered tests 01 through 07 in [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md), because every later chapter assumes they pass.

questions.question: What is a personal agent?
questions.answer: A **personal agent** is software that carries out multi-step tasks on one person's behalf, such as checking calendars, summarizing information, and coming back when it needs a decision. The key word is *multi-step*: an agent works toward a goal, not just a single reply. For example, a personal agent might notice a biology test on Friday, check that you also have a lab report due Thursday, and remind you on Wednesday evening that both are coming. You never asked it a question; it acted on your behalf using your calendar. Most commercial personal agents are closed, run on a vendor's cloud computers, and charge a subscription. The Open Study Buddy takes the opposite approach: the agent is open, and each person, class, or school decides where it runs and which data it may touch. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md).

questions.question: What is the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
questions.answer: A **chatbot** answers one message at a time. You ask, it replies, and it waits for your next message. An **agent** plans and performs several steps toward a goal, often using tools such as a calendar lookup, and it may come back to you when it needs a decision. A useful test: a chatbot can explain what a calendar is, but an agent reads *your* calendar and tells you what is due. At Level 3 of the book's agent progression, the buddy can answer "Do I have anything big coming up?" and then offer "I can set a reminder for Thursday at 7 pm. Should I?", using **agent approval rules** before it acts. Many products marketed as "AI assistants" are really chatbots. The [Chatbot or Agent Sorter](sims/chatbot-or-agent-sorter/index.md) lets you practice telling them apart. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md).

questions.question: What is the difference between a cloud agent, a self-hosted agent, and a school-hosted agent?
questions.answer: The difference is *who runs the computer the agent thinks on*, and therefore who controls its data and settings. - A **cloud agent** runs on a vendor's remote computers, is reached over the internet, and usually costs a recurring fee. The vendor stores your data and sets the rules. - A **self-hosted agent** runs on computers you or your school control, so the owner chooses its settings and which data it may touch. - A **school-hosted agent** is a self-hosted agent run by a school on its own equipment, under school rules for data and configuration, for example a Raspberry Pi in the library connected to the school calendar. The trade-offs are cost, control, latency, and data exposure. A cloud agent may be more capable out of the box, but student questions leave the building. A school-hosted agent keeps data local and costs nothing per month, but the school maintains it. The [Agent Hosting Trade-Off Explorer](sims/agent-hosting-tradeoff-explorer/index.md) compares the three. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md).

questions.question: What is the buddy server?
questions.answer: The **buddy server** is a program on the school network that receives requests from the device and returns replies. It is where the agent's "brain" lives. The Pico records, displays, and speaks; the buddy server decides what to say. In [Chapter 13](chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/index.md) the server is `buddy_server.py`, about 190 lines of Python's standard library, so there is nothing to install. It has two endpoints: an HTTP POST to `/v1/ask` runs the brain on a question and `GET /v1/health` reports that the server is up. It validates every request against the contract and returns clear errors such as 400 for bad JSON or 413 for an oversize body. The brain itself is one function, `decide()`, first written in [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md). Later chapters swap what is inside that function, adding speech services in [Chapter 14](chapters/14-streaming-security-resilience/index.md) and the school calendar in [Chapter 16](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md), without changing the Pico code.

questions.question: What is the request-reply contract?
questions.answer: The **request-reply contract** is the small, fixed message format that the device and the buddy server agree on. Because both sides follow it, either side can be replaced without changing the other. A request has exactly three fields and so does a reply: ```json {"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"} ``` ```json {"speak": "Your next test is Biology on Friday.", "show": "Biology test: Friday", "next_mode": "clock"} ``` The Pico sends `speak` to the speaker, puts `show` (30 characters or fewer) on the display, and switches to the mode in `next_mode`. It never needs to know whether the reply came from a few rules, an LLM, or a full agent framework. That is what makes the brain swappable. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md), where the contract is introduced, and [Chapter 13](chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/index.md), where it is defined for real.

questions.question: What is a swappable brain?
questions.answer: A **swappable brain** is a design in which the software that produces answers can be exchanged for another without changing the device code. On the Open Study Buddy, the brain lives entirely on the buddy server behind the request-reply contract, so replacing a rule-based server with an LLM-backed one leaves every line of Pico code untouched. This matters for three reasons. First, students can finish a working device with a simple, understandable brain before adding AI. Second, a school can choose its brain based on cost, privacy, and capability, and change its mind later. Third, it keeps the Pico's tiny memory focused on audio and display work instead of on language processing. For example, at Level 1 the question "Do I have anything big this week?" gets "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates." At Level 2 the same Pico gets "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday." See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md) and the [Study Buddy Architecture Explorer](sims/study-buddy-architecture-explorer/index.md).

questions.question: How does a spoken question travel through the system?
questions.answer: The **agent data flow** is the path information takes from your voice to the reply: 1. You hold **Mode**, and the INMP441 microphone samples your voice 12,800 times per second and sends the numbers to the Pico over I2S. 2. The Pico records the utterance, using a level gate to find where speech starts and stops. 3. The Pico sends the audio in chunks over Wi-Fi to the buddy server. 4. The server runs speech-to-text, then the brain decides on a reply, then text-to-speech turns it into audio. 5. The reply comes back as `speak`, `show`, and `next_mode`. 6. The Pico shows the text on the round display and plays the answer through the MAX98357A amplifier and speaker. At Level 1, with no speech services, the request carries text instead of audio, but the shape of the trip is the same. Tracing this flow is also how you reason about privacy: every arrow is a place where data could be stored or exposed. Step through it with the [Agent Data Flow Step-Through](sims/agent-data-flow-step-through/index.md). See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md) and [Chapter 17](chapters/17-privacy-responsible-listening/index.md).

questions.question: What is push-to-talk and why is it the default?
questions.answer: **Push-to-talk** is a listening mode in which the device listens only while a button is held. On the Open Study Buddy you hold the **Mode button**, ask your question, and release. Releasing after at least 0.2 seconds moves the device to the THINKING mode; a shorter tap is treated as an accidental press and returns to the clock. It is the default because it is the most privacy-respecting way to build a listening device. The microphone is open only when a person deliberately chooses to speak, so nothing said in the room at other times can be captured, stored, or sent. It is also more reliable than a wake word: there are no false accepts from coughs or similar words, and no false rejects from a phrase said too fast. Everything in this book works with push-to-talk alone. Always-on wake-word listening is an advanced option that requires written approval first. See [Chapter 11](chapters/11-mic-calibration-push-to-talk/index.md) and [Chapter 17](chapters/17-privacy-responsible-listening/index.md).

questions.question: What is a wake word?
questions.answer: A **wake word** is a spoken phrase that signals the device to start listening, like the names commercial smart speakers respond to. The Open Study Buddy's default wake phrase is **"Hey Pico,"** and a school can choose its own, such as "Hey Griffin." When the wake word is enabled, the microphone runs continuously and the Pico checks every audio frame to see whether the last second of sound matches a stored template of the phrase. If the match score crosses the detection threshold, the device closes the microphone, plays a short confirmation beep, and then starts listening for the question. Wake-word listening is an **advanced option** in this book. Push-to-talk stays the default, and the wake word may be turned on only after the always-on approval process is complete. The detection itself runs entirely on the Pico, so audio does not leave the device until after the phrase is heard. See [Chapter 12: Wake-Word Detection](chapters/12-wake-word-detection/index.md).

questions.question: How does the microphone turn sound into numbers?
questions.answer: Sound is a **sound wave**: tiny pressure variations traveling through air. Its **frequency**, how many cycles it completes each second, is what we hear as pitch, and its **amplitude**, the size of the swing, is what we hear as loudness. Middle A, for example, is a 440 Hz wave. The INMP441 is a **MEMS microphone**, built from a microscopic mechanical membrane on a silicon chip. The pressure wave moves the membrane, which changes an electrical signal. A converter on the same microphone board then performs **analog to digital conversion**: it measures that signal 12,800 times per second and turns each measurement into a 24-bit number. The board sends those numbers to the Pico over the I2S bus. So by the time audio reaches your MicroPython code, it is already a list of integers. A common misconception is that the Pico does the conversion; it does not. The Pico only receives, stores, and analyzes numbers, which is why audio processing on the device is really arithmetic on arrays. See [Chapter 3](chapters/03-sound-and-digital-audio/index.md) and [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md).

questions.question: What is sampling and what is a sample rate?
questions.answer: **Sampling** is measuring a continuous signal, such as the air-pressure wave of sound, at equal time steps and keeping only those measurements. Each measurement is a **sample**, and the **sample rate** is how many samples are taken each second, measured in hertz. Think of it as photographing the height of a wave many times a second. You do not keep the wave between the photographs, only a list of heights. The kit's microphone uses a sample rate of **12,800 Hz**, so one second of sound is a list of 12,800 numbers. That rate was chosen because it is plenty for speech, it keeps the signal-processing work cheap, and with 512-sample frames it makes each frame exactly 40 ms long and gives the FFT bins exactly 25 Hz apart. The speaker tests use 16,000 Hz. See [Chapter 3: Sound and Digital Audio Basics](chapters/03-sound-and-digital-audio/index.md) and the [Sampling Explorer](sims/sampling-explorer/index.md).

questions.question: What is the Nyquist limit?
questions.answer: The **Nyquist limit** is half the sample rate. It is the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent correctly. To capture a frequency, you need more than two samples per cycle of it. For the kit's 12,800 Hz microphone, the Nyquist limit is 6,400 Hz. For the 16,000 Hz speaker tests it is 8,000 Hz. Human speech carries most of its useful information well below 6,400 Hz, which is why the kit's rate is enough for a study buddy. Frequencies above the limit do not simply disappear. They show up as false lower frequencies, an effect called **aliasing**. A tone at frequency *f* between half the sample rate and the full sample rate appears at the sample rate minus *f*. With the microphone at 12,800 Hz, a 7,000 Hz whistle appears as a 5,800 Hz tone, and once the samples are stored there is no way to tell it from a real one. See [Chapter 3](chapters/03-sound-and-digital-audio/index.md) and the [Sampling Explorer](sims/sampling-explorer/index.md).

questions.question: What is an audio frame and why is it 40 ms?
questions.answer: An **audio frame** is the fixed-size slice of audio a program processes in one pass of its loop: read a frame, analyze it, update the screen, repeat. The kit's frame is **512 samples**. At 12,800 samples per second that is exactly 512 / 12,800 = 0.04 seconds, or 40 ms. Each sample is stored in 4 bytes, so a frame is 2,048 bytes, and the loop runs 25 times a second. The frame length is a trade-off. A longer frame gives the FFT finer frequency detail but responds more slowly. A shorter frame responds faster but gives coarser detail and runs the loop more often: | Frame samples | Duration | Loop passes per second | |---------------|----------|------------------------| | 256 | 20 ms | 50 | | 512 | 40 ms | 25 | | 1,024 | 80 ms | 12.5 | The 40 ms frame also sets the **frame time budget**: everything the loop does for one frame must finish in 40 ms. See [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md) and the [Audio Frame Time Budget Explorer](sims/audio-frame-budget-explorer/index.md).

questions.question: What is the frame time budget and what happens if I go over it?
questions.answer: The **frame time budget** is the time you have to finish one pass of the loop before the next audio frame is ready. On the kit it is 40 ms. Reading, analyzing, drawing, and deciding must all fit. If a pass finishes early, `readinto()` simply waits for the rest of the frame and the loop stays in step. If a pass takes longer, that is a **frame overrun**: the microphone keeps filling its ring buffer while your code is busy, and the backlog grows. The ring holds about 9.8 frames (measured on the test board), and once the backlog passes that, audio is lost. For example, a loop that takes 50 ms per pass falls 0.25 frames behind each time and loses audio after about 2.0 seconds. A full-screen redraw at about 130 ms per pass loses audio after only about 0.65 seconds. Even a loop just 5 ms too slow loses audio within about 3.6 seconds. See [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md), [Chapter 10](chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/index.md), and the [Audio Frame Time Budget Explorer](sims/audio-frame-budget-explorer/index.md).

questions.question: What is the FFT and why does the device need it?
questions.answer: The **FFT** (fast Fourier transform) is a fast algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform, which converts a frame of samples from the **time domain** (values over time) into the **frequency domain** (how strong each frequency is). It gives the same answer as the direct calculation with roughly a hundred times less work for a 512-sample frame. Loudness alone tells the device *how much* sound there is. The FFT tells it *what kind* of sound: silence, a steady hum, a whistle, or speech. The Open Study Buddy uses the FFT for its live spectrum display, for peak-frequency detection in projects like a tuner, and for the band-energy features that drive wake-word detection. The kit's FFT takes 512 samples and produces 256 useful frequency bins, each 25 Hz wide. Those bins are grouped into 16 log-spaced bands for display and for features. See [Chapter 9: Signal Processing and the FFT](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md) and the [Time and Frequency Domain Viewer](sims/time-and-frequency-domain-viewer/index.md).

questions.question: What is a frequency bin and how do I calculate its frequency?
questions.answer: A **frequency bin** is one slot of an FFT result. It collects the energy of every sound close to one particular frequency. The **bin width** is the sample rate divided by the FFT size, and bin *k* is centered on *k* times the bin width. For the kit, the sample rate is 12,800 Hz and the FFT size is 512, so the bin width is 12,800 / 512 = **25 Hz**. Bin 1 is 25 Hz, bin 40 is 1,000 Hz, and bin 255 is 6,375 Hz. Bin 256 would be 6,400 Hz, the Nyquist limit, so the code uses bins 0 through 255. To go the other way, divide the frequency by 25. Concert A at 440 Hz gives 17.6, so it lands nearest bin 18, centered on 450 Hz. The bin width is the finest pitch distinction one frame can make: two tones closer than about 25 Hz merge, and reading a pitch off the nearest bin can be off by up to half a bin, 12.5 Hz. Practice with the [FFT Bin Calculator](sims/fft-bin-calculator/index.md). See [Chapter 9](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md).

questions.question: What is the I2S bus?
questions.answer: The **I2S bus** is a three-wire serial connection designed for digital audio. Both the INMP441 microphone and the MAX98357A amplifier connect to the Pico over I2S, each on its own set of pins. The three signals are: - **Bit clock** (SCK or BCLK): ticks once per data bit, marking when each bit is valid. - **Word select** (WS or LRC): marks the start of each sample and whether it belongs to the left or right channel. - **Serial data** (SD or DIN): carries the audio bits themselves. The microphone is wired for **I2S receive**: SCK on GP10, WS on GP11, SD on GP12. The amplifier is wired for **I2S transmit**: BCLK on GP20, LRC on GP21, DIN on GP19. MicroPython's `machine.I2S` class requires word select to be the pin right after the bit clock, which is why each pair sits on neighboring pins. See [Chapter 8: I2S Audio](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md) and the [I2S Signal Reader](sims/i2s-signal-reader/index.md).

questions.question: Why can't I just redraw the whole screen every time something changes?
questions.answer: Because the screen holds a lot of data and the link to it is slow compared with the audio clock. A 360 × 360 display has 129,600 pixels. At 2 bytes per pixel in RGB565 color, one full frame is 259,200 bytes, about 259 KB. At the fastest SPI speed of 24 MHz, sending that frame takes at least 86.4 ms, and on the test board a full-screen fill measured about 129 ms, or about 7.7 frames per second. A single full redraw therefore takes longer than three whole 40 ms audio frames. While the Pico is busy pushing pixels, the microphone keeps producing samples that no one is reading, and audio is lost. The fix is not a faster bus. It is to stop sending pixels that did not change. A clock-digit box is about 6,000 bytes and a level meter about 8,800 bytes, each of which fits easily inside an audio frame. See [Chapter 5](chapters/05-display-basics/index.md) and the [Frame Size and Update Time Calculator](sims/frame-size-calculator/index.md).

questions.question: What is a frame buffer and why doesn't the device keep one for the whole screen?
questions.answer: A **frame buffer** is a block of memory holding the color of every pixel for one screen image. On a computer, the graphics system draws into a frame buffer and then sends the whole image to the screen. The **frame size calculation** for this display is 360 × 360 pixels × 2 bytes = 259,200 bytes. That is a problem on the Pico in two ways. First, memory: the Pico 2 W has about 520 KB of RAM for everything, so a 259 KB buffer would take half of it, leaving too little for audio buffers, the FFT, and the network. Second, time: the **update bandwidth** of the SPI link means sending the whole buffer, a **full-frame update**, takes at least 86.4 ms at 24 MHz and measured about 129 ms. So the device draws directly to the display instead. The **SPI display driver** provides `fill_rect()` and `blit_buffer()`, which set a drawing window and stream only that rectangle's pixels from a small buffer. For example, a clock-digit box needs a buffer of about 6,000 bytes, not 259,200. See [Chapter 5](chapters/05-display-basics/index.md) and the [Frame Size and Update Time Calculator](sims/frame-size-calculator/index.md).

questions.question: What is a direct region write?
questions.answer: A **direct region write** sends pixels only for a chosen rectangle of the screen instead of the whole frame. The display controller supports this with a **drawing window**: the Pico sends a command that defines a rectangle, and then streams exactly that many pixels, which fill the rectangle row by row. The savings are large. Painting a 100 × 30 box one pixel at a time with `pixel()` sends 39,000 bytes and measured about 1.6 seconds on the test board. Painting the same box with one `fill_rect()` sets the window once and sends 6,011 bytes, which measured 4.3 ms, roughly 370 times faster. For a region with mixed colors, you build the pixels in a `bytearray` and send them with `blit_buffer()`. Combined with **dirty regions**, the parts of the screen that actually changed, direct region writes let the device update the clock digits, a spectrum bar, or a status icon while staying inside the audio frame budget. See [Chapter 6: Drawing Directly to Display Regions](chapters/06-display-regions-and-drawing/index.md) and the [Dirty Region Planner](sims/dirty-region-planner/index.md).

questions.question: What is a state machine and how does the device use one?
questions.answer: A **state machine** is a program structure with a fixed set of states and rules for moving between them. At every moment the machine is in exactly one state. An event, such as a button press or a reply arriving, may cause a transition to another state. The Open Study Buddy has five **device modes**: CLOCK, LISTENING, THINKING, SPEAKING, and SETTINGS. The mode decides what the screen shows and what each button does. For example, in CLOCK a Mode press starts LISTENING; in THINKING a Mode press cancels and returns to CLOCK; a reply arriving moves THINKING to SPEAKING; and speech finishing returns SPEAKING to CLOCK. The rules are written as a table, and the code is the table: one class holds the state, and one method reacts to events with one branch per state. That is how three buttons run a five-mode device without confusion. Try it in the [Device Mode State Machine](sims/device-mode-state-machine/index.md). See [Chapter 7](chapters/07-buttons-and-device-modes/index.md).

questions.question: What does MQTT do and how is it different from HTTP?
questions.answer: The **MQTT protocol** is a lightweight messaging protocol built on the **publish-subscribe pattern**. Senders publish messages to named **topics**, receivers subscribe to the topics they want, and a server called the **MQTT broker** delivers each message to every current subscriber. Publishers and subscribers never talk to each other directly. The **HTTP protocol** uses the **request-response pattern**: a client asks and a server replies. That suits a question like "When is my next test?", where the student starts the exchange. It does not suit an alert, because the server cannot start an HTTP conversation with a desk device. The device would have to keep asking ("anything new?"), which wastes time and network traffic. With MQTT, every Study Buddy keeps one connection open to the school broker and subscribes to its school and classroom alert topics. When the school publishes "Algebra II test tomorrow," every subscribed device receives it within moments. The Open Study Buddy uses both: HTTP for questions, MQTT for push alerts. See [Chapter 15: MQTT and Push Alerts](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md) and the [MQTT Topic Router](sims/mqtt-topic-router/index.md).

questions.question: Why does calendar parsing happen on the server and not on the Pico?
questions.answer: This is the rule of **server-side parsing**. An **ICS feed** in the **iCalendar format** (`.ics`) looks simple, but reading it correctly means unfolding long lines, handling time zones and daylight saving rules, expanding repeating events, and following dozens of special cases in the standard. That is hundreds of lines of code and a lot of RAM. The Pico has about 520 KB of RAM in the whole chip, and it needs that memory for audio buffers, the FFT, and the display. The buddy server, running on a computer or a Raspberry Pi, has plenty of memory and does the work once for every device in the school. What reaches a desk is already digested: a short MQTT alert with a pre-formatted `when` field like "Tomorrow 8:00 AM", or a one-sentence reply. The Pico never does calendar math. See [Chapter 16](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md) and the [ICS Line Parser Stepper](sims/ics-line-parser-stepper/index.md).

questions.question: What does it mean for the Open Study Buddy to be "open"?
questions.answer: "Open" has two parts in this book. **Open hardware** means the physical design is published and built from common parts that anyone can buy and wire without special licenses: a Pico 2 W, a round display, a microphone board, an amplifier board, buttons, and a breadboard. **Open source software** means the code is published under a license that lets people read, change, and share it. MicroPython, Mosquitto, and the book's own scripts are all open. For a personal agent, openness has a practical consequence: control. You can read every line that runs on your desk, see exactly what data leaves the device, and choose where the agent runs and what it may access. Nothing is hidden behind a vendor's servers or a subscription. This contrasts with most commercial personal agents, which are closed products hosted on the vendor's cloud. See [Chapter 1](chapters/01-personal-agents-architecture/index.md).

questions.question: Which Pico pins does each part use?
questions.answer: The kit's **pin assignment table** is the one document you wire from and debug against, and the kit's `config.py` comes from it: | Part | Signals and Pico pins | |------|------------------------| | Display (SPI) | SCL GP2, SDA GP3, RST GP4, DC GP5, CS GP6, BL (backlight) GP7, VCC to 3V3 | | Microphone (I2S receive) | SCK GP10, WS GP11, SD GP12, L/R to GND, VDD to 3V3 | | Buttons | MODE GP13, UP GP14, DOWN GP15, other legs to GND | | Amplifier (I2S transmit) | DIN GP19, BCLK GP20, LRC GP21, GAIN GP18, VIN to VBUS or 3V3 | Three rules hold the table together. Each GP pin appears once. The I2S pairs are neighbors, because word select must be the pin after the bit clock. And nothing connects to GP23, GP24, GP25, or GP29, which belong to the Pico 2 W's wireless chip. See [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md) and the [Kit Wiring Fault Finder](sims/kit-wiring-fault-finder/index.md).

questions.question: What does the machine library provide?
questions.answer: The **machine library** is the MicroPython module that gives programs direct access to the microcontroller's hardware. Almost every file in this book starts by importing something from it. The classes the Open Study Buddy uses most are: | Class | What it controls | Used for | |-------|------------------|----------| | `Pin` | A single **GPIO pin** as input or output | Buttons with pull-ups, the display backlight, the mute switch | | `SPI` | The SPI bus | Sending commands and pixels to the round display | | `I2S` | The I2S audio bus | Reading the microphone, driving the amplifier | | `Timer` | A hardware timer that fires at regular intervals | Periodic checks without blocking the loop | For example, `Pin(13, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)` makes GP13 an input with an internal pull-up resistor, which is how the Mode button is read. A `Pin` can also trigger an **interrupt** on a falling edge, running a short handler the moment the button is pressed. The kit's `config.py` wraps these calls in helper functions such as `config.init_display()`, so the pin numbers live in one place. See [Chapter 2](chapters/02-micropython-review/index.md) and the [Kit Import Map](sims/kit-import-map/index.md).

questions.question: What is RGB565 color?
questions.answer: **RGB565** is a 16-bit color format that stores each pixel in two bytes: 5 bits of red, 6 bits of green, and 5 bits of blue. Green gets the extra bit because human eyes are most sensitive to green. The round display uses RGB565, which is why one full frame is 360 × 360 × 2 = 259,200 bytes. To build a color, shift each channel into place: red occupies the top 5 bits, green the middle 6, and blue the bottom 5. Pure red is `0xF800`, pure green is `0x07E0`, pure blue is `0x001F`, white is `0xFFFF`, and black is `0x0000`. When you fill a `bytearray` for `blit_buffer()`, each color is written as two bytes, high byte first. Because each channel has fewer levels than the 8-bit-per-channel colors on a computer screen, very subtle gradients can show bands. Simple designs with strong colors look best on the device. Experiment with the [RGB565 Color Mixer](sims/rgb565-color-mixer/index.md). See [Chapter 5](chapters/05-display-basics/index.md).

questions.question: What is bit depth?
questions.answer: **Bit depth** is the number of bits used to store each sample. More bits means more possible values and finer steps between them. A 16-bit sample has 65,536 possible values; a 24-bit sample has about 16.7 million. The INMP441 microphone sends 24-bit samples, carried in 32-bit slots on the I2S bus, so the Pico stores each microphone sample in 4 bytes. That is why a 512-sample frame is 2,048 bytes. Each extra bit doubles the number of levels and adds about 6 dB of range between the quietest and loudest sounds the format can represent. Bit depth also explains **audio clipping**. When a sound is louder than the largest value the format can represent, the samples flatten at the maximum, and the result is harsh distortion that no later processing can undo. See [Chapter 3](chapters/03-sound-and-digital-audio/index.md) and the [Bit Depth Quantizer](sims/bit-depth-quantizer/index.md).

questions.question: What does machine.I2S do?
questions.answer: The **machine.I2S class** is how MicroPython sends and receives I2S audio. You create one object for the microphone in receive mode and another for the amplifier in transmit mode, giving each its pins, sample bits, format (mono or stereo), sample rate, and an internal buffer size (`ibuf`). The key method for recording is `readinto(buffer)`, which fills a `bytearray` you created once with fresh samples. It blocks until the buffer is full, which conveniently keeps a loop in step with the microphone. For playback, `write(buffer)` sends samples to the amplifier. The driver keeps its own ring buffer so audio is not lost while your code is briefly busy. On the test board, the microphone's 40,000-byte internal buffer measured about 0.4 seconds deep, roughly 9.8 frames, which is less than the arithmetic suggests; the chapter explains a likely but unconfirmed reason. See [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md).

questions.question: How does the MAX98357A amplifier drive the speaker?
questions.answer: The **MAX98357A** is an I2S digital audio amplifier on a small breakout board. The Pico uses **I2S transmit** to send it a stream of samples on three wires (DIN GP19, BCLK GP20, LRC GP21). The chip converts those numbers back into an electrical signal strong enough to move the **speaker** cone, so the whole path from sample to sound is digital until the last stage. It is a **Class-D amplifier**, which means its output switches fully on and off very rapidly instead of operating partly on. Switching wastes very little power as heat, so the board stays cool and runs from USB power. The Pico has two ways to give it sound. **Tone generation** builds samples for a pure frequency, such as an 880 Hz confirmation beep, usually by reading a precomputed **sine table** rather than calling `sin()` for every sample. **Stored audio playback** streams samples from a WAV file or a buffer, which is how spoken replies from the text-to-speech service are played. **Volume control** scales the samples before they are sent; the GAIN pin (GP18) sets the amplifier's gain, which the kit's `set_gain()` function picks in software, 9 dB by default. See [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md) and [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md).

questions.question: What is RMS loudness and how is it measured in decibels?
questions.answer: **RMS loudness** (root mean square) measures a signal's strength: square every sample, average the squares, and take the square root. Squaring makes negative and positive swings count equally, so RMS reflects how much energy the sound has. A louder room produces a higher RMS value. Before computing it, the code removes the **DC offset**, the average value of the frame, so the signal centers on zero. Otherwise a constant offset would look like loudness. **Decibels** convert RMS into a logarithmic scale that matches how we hear. Doubling the amplitude adds about 6 dB. The book often reports levels as dBFS, decibels relative to full scale, where 0 dBFS is the largest value the format can hold and quieter sounds are negative. The Chapter 11 calibration also works in "bits" of loudness, a closely related log scale. A **volume meter** on the display is simply a bar whose length follows RMS loudness, frame by frame. See [Chapter 9](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md).

questions.question: What is windowing and why does the FFT need a Hann window?
questions.answer: The FFT assumes the frame it receives repeats forever. A real 40 ms frame almost never starts and ends at the same value, so the FFT sees an abrupt jump at the edges. That jump smears a pure tone's energy into neighboring bins, an effect called **spectral leakage**. **Windowing** fixes this by multiplying the frame by a smooth shape that tapers to zero at both ends before the FFT. The **Hann window** is a bell-shaped curve commonly used for this. After windowing, the frame starts and ends at zero, the edge jump disappears, and a pure tone shows up as a narrow peak instead of a wide smear. The cost is a small loss of precision in exactly where a peak sits and how tall it is, which the book handles with peak-frequency refinement. For speech and spectrum displays, the cleaner picture is well worth it. See the leakage with and without a window in the [Spectral Leakage Explorer](sims/spectral-leakage-explorer/index.md). See [Chapter 9](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md).

questions.question: What are log-spaced bands?
questions.answer: **Log-spaced bands** are frequency ranges whose widths grow with frequency, so each band covers roughly the same musical interval, such as an octave, rather than the same number of hertz. This matches human hearing, which perceives the step from 100 Hz to 200 Hz as about as large as the step from 1,000 Hz to 2,000 Hz. The FFT produces 256 bins, each 25 Hz wide, which are evenly spaced. Drawing 256 bars would be unreadable on a round display, and evenly spaced groups would waste most bars on high frequencies where speech has little detail. So the kit groups the bins into **16 log-spaced bands** and sums each band's energy. Low bands contain only a few bins and high bands contain many. The resulting 16 **band energies** drive the live spectrum display, and the same 16 numbers per frame are the features used for wake-word detection. Arrange bands yourself with the [Log Band Layout Explorer](sims/log-band-layout-explorer/index.md). See [Chapter 9](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md).

questions.question: What is a magnitude spectrum and how does it become a spectrum display?
questions.answer: The FFT produces one complex number per frequency bin. The **magnitude spectrum** is the list of how strong each bin is, found from the size of each complex number. For the kit, that is 256 magnitudes, one per 25 Hz bin, for every 40 ms frame. Raw magnitudes are hard to display because loud and quiet frequencies differ by huge factors. **Log magnitude** converts them to a logarithmic scale, usually decibels, so a soft consonant and a loud vowel both show up as visible bars. **Peak frequency detection** finds the bin with the largest magnitude, which is how a tuner or whistle detector reports a pitch. The **spectrum display** on the round screen groups the 256 bins into 16 log-spaced bands and draws one bar per band, redrawing only the bars that changed. A **spectrogram** goes one step further and shows how the spectrum changes over time, with color for strength and time scrolling sideways. For example, a steady whistle shows one tall bar that stays put, while speech shows several bars that rise and fall quickly as vowels and consonants change. See [Chapter 9](chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/index.md).

questions.question: What is viper code?
questions.answer: **Viper code** is MicroPython that is compiled to real machine instructions for the processor instead of being interpreted. You mark a function with the `@micropython.viper` decorator and add type hints to its arguments. Inside, integers are plain 32-bit machine words that wrap around instead of growing, array arguments become pointers (`ptr8`, `ptr16`, `ptr32`) into your memory, and nothing is allocated. That makes viper well suited to the inner loops of audio processing, such as windowing a frame or the FFT's butterflies. The book's `window_viper()` multiplies each 16-bit sample by a Q15 window value with no object creation at all. Viper has rules. There are no default argument values, floating point is not optimized, pointers have no bounds checking and no slices, and a `ptr16` read returns an unsigned value that you must convert if your samples are signed. An index that is too large silently overwrites memory beyond the array. See [Chapter 10: High-Performance MicroPython](chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/index.md) and the [Speed-Up Chooser](sims/speedup-chooser/index.md).

questions.question: What is Q15 fixed-point math?
questions.answer: **Fixed-point math** uses integers with an implied decimal point to represent fractions, so the processor can use fast integer instructions instead of slower floating-point ones. **Q15** is a common format in which a signed 16-bit integer represents a value from -1 up to just under +1, with 15 bits after the binary point. The integer 32,767 stands for about 0.99997, 16,384 for 0.5, and -32,768 for -1.0. To multiply two Q15 numbers, multiply the integers to get a 30-bit-scaled result and then shift right by 15 bits to bring it back to Q15. Window values and FFT twiddle factors are all between -1 and +1, so Q15 suits them naturally. The cost is precision and range: results must stay inside -1 to +1 or they overflow, and each operation rounds slightly. Chapter 10 checks how accurate the viper Q15 FFT is compared with a floating-point version. Convert values with the [Q15 Calculator](sims/q15-calculator/index.md). See [Chapter 10](chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/index.md).

questions.question: How does the debounce and long-press logic work?
questions.answer: Mechanical buttons **bounce**: when the contacts meet, they spring apart and touch several times in a few milliseconds, making the pin flicker before it settles. **Button debouncing** ignores any further change for a short time after accepting one. The kit's test uses 30 ms. Too short and a noisy switch gets through; too long and two quick taps merge into one. The buttons are wired with a **pull-up**, so a pin reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed. A press is a **falling edge** from 1 to 0. A **long press** gives a button a second job. The code remembers when the press started, and if the button is still down after 800 ms it sends a "long" event, once. The book's `Button` class returns three events: `"press"` at the falling edge, `"long"` at 800 ms, and `"release"` with the hold time. Always compare times with `time.ticks_diff()`, never plain subtraction, because the millisecond counter wraps around. See the [Button Bounce and Debounce Visualizer](sims/debounce-bounce-visualizer/index.md) and [Chapter 7](chapters/07-buttons-and-device-modes/index.md).

questions.question: What do the Mode, Up, and Down buttons do in each mode?
questions.answer: Each button's meaning depends on the current mode. "Short" means released before 800 ms; "long" means held 800 ms or more. | Mode | MODE | UP | DOWN | |------|------|----|------| | CLOCK | press: start LISTENING | short: volume up; long: SETTINGS | short: volume down | | LISTENING | release after 0.2 s or more: THINKING; sooner: CLOCK | ignored | ignored | | THINKING | press: cancel to CLOCK | ignored | ignored | | SPEAKING | press: stop to CLOCK | volume up | volume down | | SETTINGS | short: next setting; long: CLOCK | raise value | lower value | Two events are not buttons: a full recording buffer moves LISTENING to THINKING, and a reply arriving moves THINKING to SPEAKING. Pressing Mode while the device is speaking is a **barge-in interruption**, which stops the reply. Mode is never long-pressed in LISTENING because you hold it while talking. See [Chapter 7](chapters/07-buttons-and-device-modes/index.md).

questions.question: What are MQTT QoS levels and which ones does the book use?
questions.answer: The **QoS level** (quality of service) is the delivery promise for one message: | QoS | Promise | If a packet is lost | |-----|---------|---------------------| | 0 | At most once | The message is gone | | 1 | At least once | It is resent, so it may arrive twice | | 2 | Exactly once | A four-step handshake prevents repeats, at extra cost | A message reaches a subscriber at the *lower* of the publish QoS and the subscribe QoS. MicroPython's `umqtt.simple` supports QoS 0 and 1, not 2. The book pays for a stronger promise only where it matters. Alerts use QoS 1, because losing a test notice is worse than seeing it twice, and each alert's `id` lets the device ignore a repeat. Online and offline status uses QoS 1 and is retained. Telemetry such as volume and uptime uses QoS 0, because the next report replaces it in 30 seconds. Step through the packets in the [QoS Handshake Stepper](sims/mqtt-qos-handshake-stepper/index.md). See [Chapter 15](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md).

questions.question: What are retained messages and last will?
questions.answer: A **retained message** is one the broker stores for a topic and hands immediately to any new subscriber. If a device reboots or joins late, it does not have to wait for the next publish to learn the current state. The book retains each device's online/offline status so a teacher's dashboard always shows the latest value. A **last will** is a message a client registers with the broker when it connects. If the client disconnects unexpectedly, because power is cut or Wi-Fi drops, the broker publishes the last will on the client's behalf. The Study Buddy's last will reports it offline on its `status` topic. The broker detects a silent client through the **keep-alive**: the client promises to send something at least every interval, and if the broker hears nothing for about one and a half intervals, it declares the client gone and sends the will. Together, retained status plus last will give a dashboard an accurate list of which desks are online without any polling. See [Chapter 15](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md).

questions.question: How are MQTT topics named in this book?
questions.answer: A **topic** is a slash-separated string, like a folder path, that labels a message. The book's **topic naming scheme** goes from general to specific, with the school id first: | Topic | Published by | Read by | |-------|--------------|---------| | `school/<school>/alert` | buddy server | every device in the school | | `school/<school>/class/<room>/alert` | buddy server | devices in that room | | `school/<school>/device/<device>/status` | the device, and the broker for its last will | dashboards, the teacher | | `school/<school>/device/<device>/telemetry` | the device | dashboards | Putting the school first lets one broker serve two schools and lets access rules be written per school. Devices write only under their own `device/<id>/` branch, so the broker can stop a confused or stolen device from speaking for another. Every level uses lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens; "Lab 130" becomes `lab-130`. Subscriptions can use **wildcards**: `+` matches exactly one level and `#` matches everything below. A dashboard subscribing to `school/crhs/device/+/status` sees every device. Try the rules in the [MQTT Topic Router](sims/mqtt-topic-router/index.md). See [Chapter 15](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md).

questions.question: What does an MQTT alert message look like?
questions.answer: The **alert message format** is one small JSON object of strings, small because the Pico reads it into RAM and plain because schools, apps, and dashboards all read it: ```json {"id":"20261019-crhs-018-d1","type":"test","title":"Algebra II test","when":"Tomorrow 8:00 AM","text":"Algebra II test tomorrow at 8 AM. Room 118.","at":"2026-10-20T13:00Z"} ``` The `id` (up to 40 characters) is unique per alert, and the device ignores an id it has already seen. The `type` is one of `test`, `due`, `event`, `notice`, or `briefing` and chooses the color and sound. The `title` and `when` fields are each limited to 30 characters, because the message region holds two lines of 30 characters. The `when` field is already formatted by the server, so the Pico never does calendar math. The `text` field, up to 120 characters, is what a speaker would say. The whole object may not exceed 512 bytes; this one is 173. See [Chapter 15](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md).

questions.question: What are the TEST: and DUE: prefixes?
questions.answer: The **TEST and DUE prefixes** are title conventions in the school calendar that let a simple rule-based server tell which events are tests and which are project due dates. For example, a teacher or office writes `TEST: Algebra II Unit 3 - Quadratics` or `DUE: History poster`, and the server classifies the event from the start of its title. Before a school connects a real calendar, the same prefixes work in a hand-edited **events JSON file**, `events.json`, which is step one in Chapter 16. This keeps the system simple and robust. The school does not need special calendar software or extra fields; any calendar program that can export an iCalendar feed works. The rule-based buddy at Level 1 can answer "When is my next test?" by finding the next event whose title starts with `TEST:`, with no language model involved. The prefixes also choose the alert type, which sets the color and sound on the device. In the example Cedar Ridge feed, events also carry an iCalendar `CATEGORIES:TEST` line, but the title prefix is the convention people can see and edit. See [Chapter 16](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md) and the [Daily Briefing Composer](sims/daily-briefing-composer/index.md).

questions.question: How does wake-word template correlation work?
questions.answer: The detector compares the last second of sound with a stored **template** of "Hey Pico," using a few steps: 1. **Feature extraction:** each 40 ms frame becomes 16 band energies. 2. **Rolling window:** the detector keeps the most recent 25 frames, one second of features. 3. **Mean subtraction:** it subtracts the average so loudness alone cannot raise the score. 4. **Unit normalization:** it scales the window to length one so scores fall between -1 and +1. 5. **Dot product score:** it multiplies matching values of the window and template and adds them. A score near 1 means a close match. The detector fires when the score reaches the **detection threshold**, a starting value of 0.70 that you tune from your own measurements. It scores only when the window is full and at least 8 of the 25 frames passed the level gate, so a quiet room cannot correlate by accident. See the [Template Score Explorer](sims/template-score-explorer/index.md) and [Chapter 12](chapters/12-wake-word-detection/index.md).

questions.question: What is voice activity detection?
questions.answer: **Voice activity detection** (VAD) decides, frame by frame, whether the audio contains speech. The Open Study Buddy uses it to find the **utterance boundaries**, where a spoken question starts and stops, so that **recording an utterance** keeps the words and trims the silence around them. The kit's VAD is built from loudness, not from understanding words. Calibration measures the room's **noise floor** and your **speech level**. The **speech floor gate** is placed 40 percent of the way between them, and never closer than 1 bit above the noise ceiling. A high **signal-to-noise ratio**, speech well above the noise, makes this easy; a noisy room or a quiet voice makes it harder. The **level gate** applies that threshold to each 40 ms frame with hysteresis: it opens at the open level and closes only below a lower close level, so a voice hovering near the line does not flutter. For example, with a floor of 13.0 bits and a speech level of 17.0 bits, the gate opens at 14.6 and closes at 14.1. Silence after speech marks the end of the utterance. Find boundaries yourself in the [VAD Boundary Finder](sims/vad-boundary-finder/index.md). See [Chapter 11](chapters/11-mic-calibration-push-to-talk/index.md).

questions.question: How does the Pico join the Wi-Fi network?
questions.answer: The Pico 2 W has a **Wi-Fi radio**, a separate wireless chip on the board, which is why GP23, GP24, GP25, and GP29 are reserved for it. To join the classroom network, the device uses **network station mode**, in which it connects to an existing access point as a client: ```python import network wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF) wlan.active(True) wlan.connect(secrets.wifi_ssid, secrets.wifi_pass) ``` The program then waits, with a timeout, until `wlan.isconnected()` is true, and reads its **IP address** from `wlan.ifconfig()`. A **Wi-Fi connection** can fail for ordinary reasons, such as a wrong password, a weak signal, or a network that is restarting, so the connect step catches exceptions and retries rather than crashing. Once connected, the Pico is on the **local network** and can reach the buddy server by its IP address, such as `192.168.1.50`, which goes in `BUDDY_HOST`. Finding the server by a name like `buddy.local` with **mDNS discovery** is convenient on computers, but the book found no documentation that the Pico's MicroPython resolves mDNS names, so use the numeric address. The display's status region shows the link state so the student always knows whether the device is online. See [Chapter 13](chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/index.md).

questions.question: What is the cycle counter and how do I measure code speed?
questions.answer: The **cycle counter** is a hardware register that counts processor clock cycles. On the Pico 2's Cortex-M33 cores it is provided by the **DWT timer**, a debug unit. Reading the counter before and after a piece of code tells you exactly how many cycles it took, which is more precise than milliseconds for very short routines. For most work, `time.ticks_us()` is enough: record the time, run the code, and use `time.ticks_diff()` to get microseconds. The book uses this to compare each pass of the loop against its 40,000 µs budget. Two kinds of measurement answer different questions. **Benchmarking** asks "how fast can this code go?" and reports the best of many controlled runs. **Timing verification** asks "can this ever be late?" and reports the worst. Chapter 10's live-loop test passes only if there are no overruns and the worst pass is within 30 ms. See [Chapter 10](chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/index.md).

questions.question: My microphone is silent. How do I find the problem?
questions.answer: Work from the outside in, one cause at a time. 1. **Power:** the INMP441 is a 3.3 V part. Check that VDD goes to 3V3, not VBUS. A 5 V supply can damage it. 2. **Ground and channel select:** L/R and GND must both go to ground. L/R to ground selects the left channel, which is what the code reads. 3. **I2S pins:** SCK must be GP10, WS GP11, and SD GP12. If WS is on the wrong pin, `I2S()` raises an error saying word select must be the pin after SCK, but a swapped SD wire just gives silence or noise. 4. **Configuration:** check that the code uses receive mode, the right sample rate, and mono format. 5. **Mute switch:** if your build has a hardware mute switch, make sure it is not cutting power. Run the microphone probe or kit test 06, which shows a level meter that should move when you talk. A probe that prints numbers tells you more than an error message, because many wiring mistakes produce no error at all. Practice with the [Diagnosis Decision Tree Trainer](sims/diagnosis-decision-tree-trainer/index.md). See [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md) and [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md).

questions.question: My display is blank. What should I check?
questions.answer: A blank display almost always comes down to power, the backlight, wiring, or initialization. 1. **Backlight:** the BL pin must connect to GP7, and the code must turn it on. With BL disconnected, the screen stays dark even though the controller is drawing. 2. **Power and ground:** VCC to 3V3 and GND to a Pico ground. 3. **SPI wiring:** SCL GP2, SDA GP3, RST GP4, DC GP5, CS GP6. A swapped DC or CS pin usually gives a dark or garbled screen with no error message. 4. **Initialization:** confirm that `config.init_display()` ran without an exception and that the reset pin was toggled. 5. **Drawing:** a small test, such as kit test 04's "Hello World!" inside a cyan ring, removes your own code from the question. If test 04 works but your program does not, the problem is in your program, not the hardware. Common culprits are drawing outside the 360 × 360 area or a `blit_buffer()` whose buffer size does not equal width × height × 2. See [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md) and [Chapter 5](chapters/05-display-basics/index.md).

questions.question: My speaker sounds crackly or distorted. Why?
questions.answer: Distorted audio usually has one of four causes. - **Clipping:** samples that reach the maximum value flatten the waveform and sound harsh. Lower the amplitude of generated tones or the playback volume, and check the GAIN pin setting. - **Buffer underruns:** if the loop does not refill the amplifier's buffer in time, playback stutters. A slow display update or a garbage collection pause during playback is a common trigger. - **Wrong format:** a sample rate, bit depth, or mono/stereo setting that does not match the data plays at the wrong speed or as noise. - **Power supply noise:** display activity and Wi-Fi bursts can add hum or clicks. Good, short ground wiring helps, and powering the amplifier's VIN from VBUS gives it more headroom. To isolate the cause, play a known clean sine tone, such as kit test 05's beep, scale, and three volumes. If the tone is clean, the problem is in your audio data or timing; if it is not, look at wiring, gain, and power. See [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md) and [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md).

questions.question: Why do my button presses count twice or get missed?
questions.answer: Double counts are almost always **bounce**. A mechanical switch flickers between 1 and 0 for a few milliseconds when pressed, and a fast loop sees every flicker as a new press. Accept a change only if more than the debounce time, 30 ms in the kit test, has passed since the last accepted change. Missed presses usually come from one of three causes. First, a loop that blocks, for example during a full-screen redraw or a long network request, may not look at the buttons at all during a short tap. Keep the loop non-blocking, or use a **button interrupt** whose handler only sets a flag. Second, a debounce time that is too long merges two quick taps into one. Third, a wiring error: if the button's other leg goes to 3V3 instead of GND, a pulled-up pin always reads 1 and never reports a press. Run kit test 03, which prints every press and release and then "PASS." See [Chapter 7](chapters/07-buttons-and-device-modes/index.md) and the [Pull-Up Button Circuit](sims/pull-up-button-circuit/index.md).

questions.question: Why does the device hear its own voice?
questions.answer: This is the **self-hearing problem**: the microphone sits a few centimeters from the speaker, so when the device speaks, the microphone picks up its own reply. A wake-word detector might score its own beep, or push-to-talk might record the end of the last answer as part of a new question. The fix is a simple rule: **never have the microphone open while the speaker is playing.** The device closes or ignores the microphone before it plays anything, waits for the speaker's buffer to drain, and then reopens the microphone. The wake-word detector does exactly this around its confirmation beep, and then resets its window so the beep's echo cannot be scored. As an optional extension, you can wire the amplifier's shutdown pin (labeled SD on the MAX98357A board) to a spare pin such as GP22 and drive it low to switch the amplifier off completely while the device listens, which also removes any faint hiss. See "Speaking Without Hearing Yourself" in [Chapter 8](chapters/08-i2s-audio/index.md) and [Chapter 12](chapters/12-wake-word-detection/index.md).

questions.question: Why do I get a MemoryError even though there is free memory?
questions.answer: That is **heap fragmentation**. MicroPython's heap holds all your objects, and as a program creates and frees objects of different sizes, the free space gets split into small gaps between live objects. A large request, such as a 150 KB recording buffer, needs one *unbroken* block. The allocation can fail even when the total free memory is larger than the request, because no single gap is big enough. The Pico 2 W has about 520 KB of RAM for everything, so big buffers are risky. A 3-second recording at the kit's rate is 153,600 bytes, roughly 29 percent of the chip's RAM. The fixes are habits: - **Allocate big buffers once, early**, at startup, before the heap fragments. - **Reuse them** with `readinto()` and `memoryview` slices instead of creating new ones. - **Avoid allocation in loops**: no string building, list slicing, or float math in time-critical code. - Call `gc.collect()` before a large allocation if you must make one later. See the [Heap Fragmentation Explorer](sims/heap-fragmentation-explorer/index.md) and [Chapter 2](chapters/02-micropython-review/index.md).

questions.question: Why does audio glitch every few seconds?
questions.answer: Periodic glitches usually mean a **frame overrun** that happens on a schedule. Something the loop does only occasionally takes long enough to push one pass past the 40 ms budget. Common culprits are: - **Garbage collection pauses**, triggered when code allocates objects inside the loop until the heap fills. - **A full-screen redraw**, which takes about 129 ms, more than three audio frames. - **A blocking network call**, such as an HTTP request without a timeout or a `umqtt.robust` reconnect. - **Flash writes**, such as saving a cache or log file. Count overruns with a **frame overrun counter** and measure the worst pass with `time.ticks_us()`. If the counter rises steadily, the loop is too slow on average. If it jumps occasionally, find the periodic task. One slow pass costs latency, because the ring buffer catches up, but a loop that is slow on average never recovers and loses audio. See [Chapter 18](chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/index.md), [Chapter 10](chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/index.md), and the [Frame Budget Scheduler Timeline](sims/frame-budget-scheduler-timeline/index.md).

questions.question: The Pico cannot reach the buddy server. What should I check?
questions.answer: Check each link in the chain in order. 1. **Wi-Fi:** confirm `wlan.isconnected()` is true and print the Pico's IP address. Check the network name and password in your secrets file. 2. **Same network:** the Pico and the server must be on the same local subnet. A Pico at `192.168.1.37` with netmask `255.255.255.0` can reach `192.168.1.50` directly but not `192.168.2.50`. Guest networks often isolate devices from each other. 3. **Server running:** start `buddy_server.py` and note the address it prints. Put that address in `BUDDY_HOST`. 4. **Health check:** request `GET /v1/health` first. It needs no token and should return 200. 5. **Firewall:** the server computer's firewall may block incoming connections on the server's port. 6. **Token:** a 401 reply means the token is missing or wrong, and retrying will not help. The [Same-Subnet Checker](sims/same-subnet-checker/index.md) lets you practice step 2. See [Chapter 13](chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/index.md) and [Chapter 14](chapters/14-streaming-security-resilience/index.md).

questions.question: Why does the wake word trigger by accident, or not at all?
questions.answer: A detection when nobody said "Hey Pico" is a **false accept**. Saying the phrase and being ignored is a **false reject**. Both come from the same setting, the **detection threshold**. Lowering it catches more real phrases but also more coughs and similar words. Raising it does the opposite. This is the **threshold trade-off**, and no threshold makes both errors zero. Common causes of false rejects are speaking faster or slower than during enrollment (**speaking pace sensitivity**), standing farther from the microphone, a different person's voice (**single-speaker limits**), or too few loud frames for the level gate. Common causes of false accepts are words that share vowel shapes with the template and a threshold set too low. The fix is to measure, not guess. Enroll carefully, recording "Hey Pico" several times at your normal pace and distance, then run `08-threshold-sweep.py` and choose a threshold from your own false-accept and false-reject counts. Explore the trade-off in the [Threshold Trade-Off Explorer](sims/threshold-tradeoff-explorer/index.md). See [Chapter 12](chapters/12-wake-word-detection/index.md).

questions.question: Push-to-talk cuts off the beginning or end of my question. Why?
questions.answer: Push-to-talk recording uses a **level gate** to find the **utterance boundaries**, where speech starts and stops. If the gate opens too late, the first soft sound of a word, like the "h" in "how," is lost. If it closes too early, the last word is cut off. The usual cause is a gate set from the wrong calibration. Re-run **microphone calibration** in the room where the device will live. The calibration measures the **noise floor** with nobody speaking, then your **speech level** while you read a sentence, and places the gate 40 percent of the way from the floor to the speech level. The gate uses **hysteresis**: it opens at one level and closes only at a lower one, so a voice hovering near the line does not make it flutter. Also check the **mic distance effect**. Speaking from across the desk is much quieter than speaking at 20 cm, so stay at the distance you calibrated at. Explore with the [Level Gate Hysteresis Explorer](sims/level-gate-hysteresis-explorer/index.md) and the [VAD Boundary Finder](sims/vad-boundary-finder/index.md). See [Chapter 11](chapters/11-mic-calibration-push-to-talk/index.md).

questions.question: Why do my two devices keep disconnecting each other from MQTT?
questions.answer: Every MQTT client must use a **client id** that is unique on the broker. When a new client connects with an id that is already in use, the broker disconnects the older one. If two Study Buddies share an id, typically because `secrets.py` was copied from one device to another, each one's reconnect kicks the other off, and the pair fight in an endless loop. Give every device its own `device_id` and use it as the MQTT client id and user name. The same id also appears in the device's topics, such as `school/crhs/device/desk-07/status`, so a unique id keeps status reports and access rules correct too. A related issue: if a device's status flips to offline and back repeatedly even with unique ids, the device may not be calling `check_msg()` or sending traffic often enough to satisfy its keep-alive interval. See [Chapter 15](chapters/15-mqtt-push-alerts/index.md).

questions.question: Why is my calendar event showing the wrong time?
questions.answer: Almost always this is a **time zone** problem. An iCalendar feed can write times three ways: in UTC (ending in `Z`), with a named zone (`DTSTART;TZID=America/Chicago:20261020T080000`), or as "floating" local time with no zone. Code that ignores the zone, or converts it wrongly around a daylight saving change, shifts events by one or more hours. The book's rule is to handle all of this on the server. The school's `agent.toml` names its time zone, such as `America/Chicago`. The server converts every event correctly, including the twice-yearly daylight saving shifts, and sends the device a pre-formatted `when` string like "Tomorrow 8:00 AM." The Pico never does calendar math, so it cannot get it wrong. If times are still wrong, check that the server computer's own clock is correct and that the school's time zone setting is right. The [Time Zone and UTC Converter](sims/school-time-utc-converter/index.md) lets you practice the conversions. See [Chapter 16](chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/index.md).

questions.question: What is the best order to wire and test the kit?
questions.answer: Wire one part, test it, then add the next. Do not wire all five parts and then run everything. When a test fails, you then know the problem is in the part you just added. The kit's numbered tests follow this order: | Test | Wire first | What to look for | |------|-----------|------------------| | 01 | Nothing | The Pico's onboard LED blinks | | 02 | Anything you have | No warnings for the parts you wired | | 03 | The three buttons | Each press and release prints, then "PASS" | | 04 | The display | "Hello World!" inside a cyan ring | | 05 | Amplifier and speaker | A beep, a scale, three volumes | | 06 | Microphone | The meter moves when you talk | | 07 | Everything | Hold MODE, talk, hear it back | Compare every wire with the pin assignment table as you go. Many wiring mistakes produce no error message; they just make a part silent or dark. The [Kit Wiring Fault Finder](sims/kit-wiring-fault-finder/index.md) gives you practice spotting the one wrong wire in a listing. See [Chapter 4](chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/index.md).

questions.question: How should I plan the screen layout?
questions.answer: Divide the screen into a **region layout**: separate rectangles that each update independently. A typical Study Buddy screen has regions for the time, the mascot, the spectrum, the agent's message, and a status bar. Each region redraws only when its own content changes and on its own schedule. Plan the schedule against the 40 ms audio frame. On the test board, redrawing the spectrum region took about 8.5 ms and ran every frame, the status bar about 3.0 ms every 200 ms, and the time region about 3.8 ms once a second.
